concepts.name: Dependency caching with keys and restore keys

questions.prompt: A workflow defines two jobs, `lint` and `test`, and neither has a `needs` key. How do they run?

choices.text: One after the other in file order, sharing one runner
In parallel, each on its own runner, with each job's steps running in order
In parallel, and the steps inside each job also run in parallel
`test` waits for `lint`, because a job depends on the job above it

questions.explanation: By default jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel, each on its own runner. Inside a job the steps run one after another on the same runner. File order means nothing: to make `test` wait for `lint` you add `needs: lint`.

sources.title: Understanding GitHub Actions
sources.claim: Jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel by default, each on its own runner VM or container, while a job's steps run in order on the same runner and can share data.

sources.title: Using jobs in a workflow
sources.claim: The needs keyword makes a job wait for the listed jobs to succeed, and if a needed job fails or is skipped the dependent job is skipped unless a condition such as always() is used.

questions.prompt: In job `build`, one step writes `dist/report.txt`. A later step in `build` reads it, and a separate job `publish` (with `needs: build`) also tries to read it from disk. What happens?

choices.text: Both find it, because every job in a workflow shares one workspace
Neither finds it, because each step runs in a fresh container
Only `publish` finds it, because files are copied once a job ends
The later step in `build` finds it; `publish` runs on another runner and doesn't

questions.explanation: Steps in one job run on the same runner, so they can share files. A different job gets its own runner, and `needs` only orders the jobs; it copies nothing. To hand a file from one job to another you pass it on explicitly, for example as an artifact.

sources.title: Understanding GitHub Actions
sources.claim: Jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel by default, each on its own runner VM or container, while a job's steps run in order on the same runner and can share data.

sources.title: Workflow artifacts
sources.claim: Artifacts persist data after a job completes so it can be shared with another job in the same workflow.

questions.prompt: Your workflow has `lint`, `test` and `deploy` jobs. `deploy` must run only after both checks pass. Explain how GitHub Actions orders jobs and steps by default, and what you change so `deploy` waits.

model_answer.summary: Jobs run in parallel by default and steps run in order within a job, so `deploy` needs `needs: [lint, test]`, which also skips it when either check fails.
key_points: By default jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel, each on its own runner
Steps inside one job run in order on the same runner
Adding `needs: [lint, test]` to `deploy` makes it wait for both jobs
If a job listed in `needs` fails, the dependent job is skipped by default

questions.explanation: A workflow is a graph of jobs, not a script. Without `needs`, GitHub starts every job at once. `needs` adds the edges: the dependent job starts only when the jobs it needs have succeeded, and is skipped when one of them fails.

sources.title: Understanding GitHub Actions
sources.claim: Jobs have no dependencies and run in parallel by default, each on its own runner VM or container, while a job's steps run in order on the same runner and can share data.

questions.prompt: You want CI to run on every pull request that targets `main`, when it's opened and each time new commits are pushed to it. Which trigger does that?

choices.text: `on: pull_request` with `branches: [main]`; by default it fires on opened, synchronize and reopened
`on: push` with `branches: [main]`; it also fires for every pull request into `main`
`on: pull_request_target`, because plain `pull_request` doesn't fire on new commits
`on: pull_request` with `types: [closed]`, which covers opening and updating

questions.explanation: With no `types`, `pull_request` fires on `opened`, `synchronize` (new commits pushed) and `reopened`. For this event the `branches` filter matches the branch the pull request targets. A `push` filter on `main` only fires when commits land on `main` itself, not for pull requests.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: By default pull_request fires on the opened, synchronize and reopened activity types, and its branches filter matches the branch the pull request targets.

questions.prompt: A workflow triggered by `pull_request_target` checks out the pull request's head commit and runs its tests. Why is this dangerous when the pull request comes from a fork?

choices.text: It isn't: `pull_request_target` runs fork code with read-only access and no secrets
The tests run against `main` instead of the pull request's code, so they prove nothing
It runs in the base repo's context, so the fork's code can reach secrets or write access
Forks can't trigger `pull_request_target`, so for fork PRs the workflow never runs

questions.explanation: `pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository's default branch, not the pull request's merge commit, and GitHub warns that running untrusted code with it can lead to cache poisoning and unintended access to write privileges or secrets. For CI on outside contributions use `pull_request`, where a fork gets no secrets and a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository's default branch, and GitHub warns that running untrusted code with it can cause cache poisoning and unintended access to secrets or write privileges.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: Except for GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets are not passed to the runner for workflows triggered from a forked repository, and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only in fork pull requests.

questions.prompt: A job's matrix is `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]` and `python: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]`, with `exclude: [{os: windows-latest, python: "3.11"}]`. How many jobs run?
questions.explanation: A matrix runs one job for every combination of its variables: 2 operating systems times 3 Python versions is 6. `exclude` removes the one combination that matches both values, leaving 5. A matrix can create at most 256 jobs per workflow run.

sources.title: Running variations of jobs in a workflow
sources.claim: A matrix runs one job for each combination of its variables, and exclude removes the listed combinations.

sources.title: Actions limits
sources.claim: A job matrix can generate at most 256 jobs per workflow run.

questions.prompt: In a 6-job test matrix with no `fail-fast` setting, the Windows / Python 3.13 job fails while the others are still running. What happens by default?

choices.text: The other jobs finish, so you see results for every combination
GitHub retries the failed job once before deciding
Only the other Windows jobs are cancelled
GitHub cancels all in-progress and queued jobs in the matrix

questions.explanation: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to `true`: when any matrix job fails, GitHub cancels every in-progress and queued job in that matrix. Set `fail-fast: false` when you want every combination's result, for example to see whether a bug is Windows-only.

sources.title: GitHub Docs source: jobs.<job_id>.strategy.fail-fast
sources.claim: strategy.fail-fast defaults to true, and when true GitHub cancels all in-progress and queued jobs in the matrix if any matrix job fails.

sources.title: Running variations of jobs in a workflow
sources.claim: With fail-fast true, if a (non-continue-on-error) matrix job fails, all jobs that are in progress or queued are cancelled.

questions.prompt: A cache step uses `key: ${{ runner.os }}-uv-${{ hashFiles('uv.lock') }}` and `restore-keys: ${{ runner.os }}-uv-`. You add a dependency, which changes `uv.lock`. What happens on the next run?

choices.text: The newest cache matching the `restore-keys` prefix is restored; a new cache is saved
The existing cache is found by prefix and updated in place with the new dependency
Nothing is restored, because only an exact `key` match can restore a cache
The step fails, because the cache key no longer matches the hash of the current lockfile

questions.explanation: The cache action first looks for an exact `key` match; failing that, it tries each `restore-keys` entry as a prefix and restores the most recent match. `cache-hit` is `false`, so a new cache is saved under the new key at the end of the job. Caches are immutable: an existing one is never updated in place.

sources.title: Dependency caching reference
sources.claim: The cache action looks for an exact key match first, then checks each restore-keys prefix in order and restores the most recently created matching cache; cache-hit is true only for an exact match.

sources.title: Dependency caching reference
sources.claim: Existing caches cannot be changed; on a miss a new cache is saved under the key when the job succeeds, so new content needs a new key.

questions.prompt: A workflow run for a pull request from `feature-x` into `main` saves a new dependency cache. Which runs can restore that cache?

choices.text: Any workflow run in the repository, on any branch
Runs on `main`, because the pull request targets it
Only re-runs of that same pull request
None: pull request runs can't save caches

questions.explanation: Cache access is scoped by branch. A cache created in a pull request can only be restored by re-runs of that pull request, and the base branch can't read it. The other direction works: a pull request run can restore caches from the base branch, which is why caching on `main` helps every pull request.

sources.title: Dependency caching reference
sources.claim: Caches are branch-scoped: a cache created by a pull request run is stored for the merge ref and can only be restored by re-runs of that pull request, while pull request runs can restore caches from the base and default branches.

questions.prompt: Your `pull_request` workflow runs an integration test that reads `${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}`. A contributor opens a pull request from their fork. What does the test get?

choices.text: The real key, masked as `***` in the logs
No key: secrets other than `GITHUB_TOKEN` aren't passed to runs triggered from a fork
The key, but only after a maintainer approves it in the secret settings
The fork owner's own repository secret with the same name

questions.explanation: With the exception of `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository, and that token is read-only there. Otherwise anyone could open a pull request that prints your keys. Design fork CI to pass without secrets, for example by skipping or mocking live API tests.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: Except for GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets are not passed to the runner for workflows triggered from a forked repository, and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only in fork pull requests.

sources.title: Secrets
sources.claim: GitHub Actions automatically redacts the contents of stored secrets printed to workflow logs.

questions.prompt: A job deploys `agent-api` to production using a cloud API key. Explain how you would store the key and gate the deploy with GitHub Actions, and what each choice protects against.

model_answer.summary: Store the key as a secret on a `production` environment with required reviewers and a branch restriction, and have only the deploy job reference that environment.
key_points: Store the key as an environment secret on a `production` environment, not in the workflow file
The deploy job opts in with `environment: production`; other jobs can't read that environment's secrets
A required-reviewers protection rule pauses the job, and it can only access the environment's secrets after the rules pass
Deployment branch rules limit which branches (for example only `main`) can deploy to the environment
Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered from forks, and GitHub redacts stored secrets it finds in logs

questions.explanation: Environments turn a secret into something you release deliberately: the secret sits behind protection rules, so no job can read it until a reviewer approves and the branch is allowed. Repository-wide secrets reach every job, which is far more exposure than a deploy key needs.

sources.title: Deployments and environments
sources.claim: Environment secrets are only available to jobs that reference the environment, a job can't access them until required reviewers approve, and deployment branch rules limit which branches can deploy.

sources.title: Events that trigger workflows
sources.claim: Except for GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets are not passed to the runner for workflows triggered from a forked repository, and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only in fork pull requests.

sources.title: Secrets
sources.claim: GitHub Actions automatically redacts the contents of stored secrets printed to workflow logs.

questions.prompt: Explain how `key` and `restore-keys` work in the GitHub Actions cache, and why a good key for Python dependencies includes a hash of the lockfile.

model_answer.summary: An exact `key` match restores that cache; otherwise `restore-keys` prefixes restore the newest partial match. Hashing the lockfile into the key makes a new cache whenever dependencies change.
key_points: The cache action first looks for an exact match of `key`; that is a cache hit
Without an exact match it tries each `restore-keys` prefix in order and restores the most recent matching cache
Caches are immutable, so a changed dependency set needs a new key rather than an update
`hashFiles('uv.lock')` in the key changes exactly when the locked dependencies change
A prefix like `${{ runner.os }}-uv-` in `restore-keys` lets a run start from an older, mostly correct cache

questions.explanation: The key should change when, and only when, the cached content would differ. A lockfile hash does that. The restore-keys fallback means a lockfile change doesn't start from nothing: the package manager downloads just the difference and a fresh cache is saved under the new key.

sources.title: Dependency caching reference
sources.claim: The cache action looks for an exact key match first, then checks each restore-keys prefix in order and restores the most recently created matching cache; cache-hit is true only for an exact match.

sources.title: Dependency caching reference
sources.claim: Existing caches cannot be changed; on a miss a new cache is saved under the key when the job succeeds, so new content needs a new key.
